A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ForgerySleuth and ForgeryAnalysis. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original manipulation localization, explanation evaluation, robustness tests, ablations, and qualitative results in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds semantic textual similarity scores, FakeShield comparisons, human evaluations, classification accuracies, and failure cases.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the same multimodal LLM, frozen SAM backbone, constrained-convolution trace encoder, three-layer fusion mechanism, training stages, and text/mask losses. The redrawn architecture and expanded explanations do not establish an algorithmic revision. Removal of authentic-image training documentation does not establish that the procedure changed.

E1.justification: The training sources, six public test datasets, ForgeryAnalysis subsets, and manipulation types remain unchanged. The added similarity scoring, human evaluation, and classification results examine existing data and capabilities; they do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FakeShield, a direct multimodal forgery-detection competitor absent from v1, across localization and explanation evaluations in Appendix C, Tables 9–12. This fills a substantive comparator gap beyond the retained traditional detectors and general multimodal models.

E3.justification: v2 adds STS evaluation using three sentence-embedding models, human scoring by 14 volunteers with 30 random samples each, and image-level classification accuracy. FakeShield evaluation introduces zero masks for images classified as real and a separate true-positive-only protocol. Existing training settings and dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: The existing component/data ablations and NIST16 distortion tests are unchanged. v2 adds focused analyses of FakeShield's missed detections versus conditional localization, qualitative comparisons, and semantic-description and small-manipulation failures. v1's short successful-example panel in Figure 6 is removed, while its detailed appendix comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.1 and the checklist newly state that stochastic evaluations are conducted twice and averaged. v1 does not specify this run count. This is additional reporting, not evidence of increased repetitions; no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance-test results are added.

E6.justification: The original localization, robustness, and ablation numbers are unchanged. New results include MiniLM-L6 STS scores of 0.926 for ForgerySleuth and 0.725 for GPT-4o, FakeShield's GPT-graded overall score of 5.55, human overall ratings of 9.44 for ForgerySleuth and 7.18 for GPT-4o, and classification accuracies of 0.989 on Columbia and 0.910 on CASIA1. These are additional evaluations, not improvements to the earlier same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same model formulation, losses, and convolution-kernel constraints. Neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the added STS evaluation introduces no new formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same framework, dataset, and data-engine contributions and claims about generalization, robustness, and explainability. The headline 24.7% localization and 35.8% explanation-score improvements are unchanged; new experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's computational-cost and evaluator limitations, Appendix E explains semantic errors despite correct localization and failures on small manipulations in complex scenes, and qualifies STS as measuring similarity rather than correctness. Appendix C attributes FakeShield's weak full-set results to missed detections and distinguishes these from conditional localization performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset counts, sources, and manipulation types in Table 8, FakeShield implementation provenance, and statements that code, data, and weights have been released, with application-controlled data access. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.2 and Figure 17's authentic-image training-text construction details are removed. Existing hardware and optimization details move to Appendix D.1 unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds FakeShield and Sentence-BERT references. Section 2.2 and Appendix C acknowledge concurrent FakeShield and explain differences in structured reasoning, expert verification, and trace-feature fusion. This is a focused positioning addition; the broader related-work account remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and affiliation edits, clarifies the data-engine description, moves implementation details and limitations into dedicated appendix sections, reorganizes the appendices, and adds a NeurIPS checklist. The main section sequence and much of the prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 switches the paper from two-column to single-column layout, redraws the dataset and architecture diagrams, and incorporates the former separate fusion diagram into Figure 3. It adds evaluation and dataset tables and new comparison/failure figures, removes two example panels, and substantially relocates and resizes retained displays.

improvement.justification: v1's explanation-quality evaluation relied on GPT-4 grading and lacked a direct multimodal forgery competitor. v2 substantially strengthens this central evidence through human evaluation, complementary STS scoring, and FakeShield comparisons, while documenting concrete failure modes. These gains improve validation and qualification of the claims, outweighing the loss of authentic-image training documentation, although statistical uncertainty remains inadequately reported.
